segments.text: „Hér er kalt,“ svarar Guðrún. „Við förum inn vegna veðursins.“

segments.text: Guðrún gefur börnunum graut. Ljós lampans er hjá henni; úti er ekkert ljós.

text: Siggi spyr: „Eru þetta ragnarök?“ Afi svarar ekki.
Í sögunni er heimurinn dimmur. Hér er bærinn dimmur líka. En saga er saga.
words_with_history.note_en: Ragnarök means the fate of the gods. Snorri also uses ragnarökkur, “twilight of the gods”, a different word. Siggi asks a frightened question; the narrator does not identify the eruption with the myth.

grammar.title: Börn Bjarna
grammar.rule: Bjarni á börn: börn Bjarna. Siggi fer til afa.
grammar.note_en:
Case is the form of a noun or pronoun that marks its job in a sentence. The genitive often identifies whose something is or what it belongs to: börn Bjarna means “Bjarni’s children”, and ljós dagsins means “the light of day”. The possessor follows the thing possessed. Bjarni becomes Bjarna; Guðrún becomes Guðrúnar. Names have their own declensions, so do not simply add English ’s. Jón becomes Jóns, Einar becomes Einars. Sonur Jóns means “Jón’s son”; dóttir Einars means “Einar’s daughter”.

A patronymic is a name identifying a parent. Sigurður Bjarnason is Sigurður, Bjarni’s son; Helga Bjarnadóttir is Helga, Bjarni’s daughter. Bjarna- is the father’s genitive. These are not shared hereditary surnames. Guðrún Einarsdóttir is Guðrún, Einar’s daughter.

A preposition also selects a case. Til means “to” and takes the genitive even though it expresses movement: til afa, “to grandfather”; til Guðrúnar, “to Guðrún”. Án means “without”: án matar, “without food”. Vegna means “because of”: vegna veðursins, “because of the weather”. Compare úr messu, “from a church service”, with the dative after úr. Movement does not by itself select the accusative: the particular preposition matters.

The definite article is attached to the noun and changes with case. Þak bæjarins means “the roof of the farmhouse”; bæjarins is the genitive of bærinn. Ljós dagsins means “the light of the day”; dagsins contains genitive -s plus article -ins. Together these give -sins. The feminine genitive article has different forms: compare bókarinnar, “of the book”, with öskunnar, “of the ash”. Learn these forms with the noun’s declension. With plural nouns the article is -nna: börn Bjarna means “Bjarni’s children”, while barnanna is barna + nna, “of the children”. In the story til barnanna means “to the children”. Do not add an English-style extra article before the possessor.

The cumulative table is a reference, not a task to memorise. The nominative names the subject; the accusative can mark an object or a destination after í; the dative can mark a location after í; the genitive can mark the possessor. The prose models bærinn, í bæinn (“into the farmhouse”), í bænum (“in the farmhouse”), and þak bæjarins (“the farmhouse’s roof”).

Bók, “book”, has genitive bókar: blaðsíðum bókarinnar means “pages of the book”. The feminine genitive article is shown by bókarinnar. The plural article appears in skó barnanna, “the children’s shoes”, and án lampanna, “without the lamps”. Strong adjective endings remain the forms already taught; this chapter does not introduce weak adjectives.

pronunciation_note.rule: In dóttir and -dóttir, tt is normally pronounced with preaspiration: a brief h-like sound before t. Read the parent’s genitive as a unit before the final part: Bjarna-son, Bjarna-dóttir, Einars-dóttir. The middle dot in the family diagram shows the name’s parts; it is not normal spelling.
